The Lanterns at Netherfield

lanternwright

Summary:

Eleven lanterns on the left, nine on the right, and one that nobody relit.

Chapter 3: The Last Lantern

Chapter Text

The lanterns along the Netherfield drive had been lit an hour before the carriages came, and by the time Elizabeth stepped down onto the gravel most of them had begun to gutter in the wind off the fields.

She counted them without meaning to. Eleven on the left, nine on the right, and one near the gate that had gone out entirely and that nobody had troubled to relight. It seemed to her a fair summary of the whole affair: a great deal of trouble taken, and one small thing left undone.

Mr. Darcy was standing beside that one, as if he had been set there to guard it.

“You are counting,” he said, when she was near enough to hear him without his raising his voice. It was not a question, and she did not answer it as one.

“I am deciding,” she said, “whether a house can be judged by its lamps. My mother would say yes. My father would say that depends on who is paying for the oil.”

He looked at the dark lantern for a long moment. Then, with a care she would not have expected of him, he took the taper from the footman’s tray, lifted the little glass door, and lit it himself.

“There,” he said. “Now you will have to judge it on something else.”

She found, walking up the steps beside him, that she did not mind the change of evidence half so much as she had supposed she would. Behind them the drive burned evenly from end to end, and for once nobody remarked on it at all.

Notes:

I rewrote this ending four times. The lantern stayed in every version.

Thank you for reading all the way to the lamps. This was written for a prompt about small kindnesses; the prompt-giver knows who they are.
